newsitem.title: USA: UPS, TEAMSTERS DIG IN AS STRIKE ENTERS 10TH DAY.
newsitem.headline: UPS, TEAMSTERS DIG IN AS STRIKE ENTERS 10TH DAY.

text.p: United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union dug in for a protracted battle as administration officials continued to monitor the 10-day strike crippling the nation's largest package carrier.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and Labor Secretary Alexis Herman weighed in on the year's biggest labor dispute Tuesday, urging both sides to work out their differences and sign a contract, but no fresh face-to-face talks were scheduled for Wednesday.

An ABC News Nightline poll released late on Tuesday showed that 40 percent of Americans were backing the union in its fight to win more higher-paying, full-time jobs for the 185,000 Teamsters who walked off their jobs last week.
UPS got only 30 percent support in the survey of 506 adults conducted Monday, while the remaining 30 percent said they were neutral.

UPS Chief Executive Officer James Kelly, in an interview on Wednesday with the Cable News Network, responded to the poll by saying, "I don't know if I can convince Americans. What I'm trying to do is convince UPS people."
The strike has already inconvenienced 26 percent of the people polled, but 64 percent opposed any intervention by President Clinton.

A cautiously optimistic Herman told reporters she expected to hear from both sides late Tuesday or Wednesday, saying each "expressed a willingness to be more flexibile in looking at their own differences."
But Kelly, when asked by CNN to characterize the state of negotiations thus far, said: "I would characterize them as being at an impasse."

"We reached impasse with the Teamsters two contracts ago. The Teamsters, at that point, sent out the ballot to our people to vote on, and they voted yes, and they kept working and they didn't lose any paychecks and our business kept on going and that's what we believe should happen this time."
The AFL-CIO federation of 78 unions on Tuesday offered millions of dollars to help Teamsters in its strike effort, while the company warned of thousands of job losses.
The Atlanta-based company took out full-page ads in dozens of newspapers to tell its story and warned the union that over 15,000 jobs would be lost if the strike lasted through Friday.

The union wants more full-time jobs because three out of five Teamsters at UPS are part-time, but UPS says the real reason for the strike is its proposal to convert the union pension fund to a UPS-based pension fund.
The company has repeatedly urged Clinton to intervene in the strike, but the president has declined, saying the work stoppage does not constitute a national emergency.
Rubin told MSNBC cable television the administration was putting "enormous" pressure on the company and the union to resolve their differences.

Clinton -- briefed Tuesday on the strike by Herman -- could ask a judge to halt the strike under the Taft-Hartly law, but the government must prove in court that the work stoppage endangers national health or safety.

Kelly said the president should step in because "it's an emergency, certainly it's an emergency for many of our customers. Whether or not it's an emergency for the entire country that's the president's decision."
Rubin noted that when the law was last invoked, 20 years ago, the courts had rejected the president's decision.
UPS wants the union to permit a vote on what it describes as its "last, best and final offer." Carey insists his union members have already voted.
UPS normally handles 12 million packages a day -- 80 percent of all packages shipped by ground nationwide -- with a work force of 301,000 people.
Schools and colleges find themselves without textbooks, and many small businesses cannot deliver their goods and are scrambling to find alternative shippers, with little luck.
